b: Gary Shteyngart’s The Sensualist, Nick Harkaway’s The Taper Man: A Novel of John Le Carré’s Circus, and Hermione Lee’s Anita Brookner: Art and Life all feature among the best reviewed books of the week.
Brought to you by Book Marks, Lit Hub’s home for book reviews.

1. The Taper Man: A Novel of John Le Carré’s Circus by Nick Harkaway
(Viking)

“The conclusion, as in most of the Circus novels, is anything but conclusive, but Harkaway exhibits his father’s knack for slow reveals, complex storylines, and salient observations about human nature. George Smiley is in good hands.”

“Slim but potent … Shapes a hideous reality into art that’s worthy of its source material: unkempt, sometimes repulsive, brutal, beautiful. You cannot look away, much less forget the things you’ve seen.”
–Lauren Christensen (The New York Times Book Review)

1 Rave • 3 Positive
Read an essay by K Chiucarello here

“Searing … From the extreme to the everyday, with mesmeric specificity, Chiucarello writes of the life that unfolds behind closed doors: both the kind of violence that leads the nanny to call 911, and her tender care of young children. Family, love, language, and the failures of all three dominate this wisely voiced, sensitively self-propelling, and continuously surprising novel.”

4. The Runner by Scarlett Thomas
(Simon & Schuster)

“Thomas is one of those novelists who would be spoken of in awed tones of admiration if only she weren’t so funny. A lot of people seem to think that literary fiction is only good if it feels like a bad time, hence the confusion of clipped sentences and dour stories with quality. The Runner has no truck with that … Thomas has fabulous control of her tone and handles the jumps between thriller, action and farce with audacious skill … As a reader, trying to keep pace with her is nothing but pleasure.”

5. Amazons: An Intimate Memoir by the First Woman Ever to Play in the National Hockey League by Cleo Birdwell
(Scribner)

“Amazons’s chapter-capping sex scenes are at once frank and endearingly chatty … Feels refreshingly out of place in 2026. At times it recalls the ambitious, chonky, libidinous fiction of the era … The freedom is thrilling, indeed out of control. Scenes go on too long, to our delight. Cleo, bless her, can’t stop. DeLillo has written his share of sturdy female characters, but never in the first person, and never so willingly.”

1. Anita Brookner: Art and Life by Hermione Lee
(Knopf)

12 Rave • 4 Positive
Read an excerpt from Anita Brookner: Art and Life here

“Offers a passionate case for studying this complex, compelling, now obscure figure … For readers who’ve ever felt similarly dismissed, the biography may spark a new passion for this connoisseur of women’s interior lives, a writer who could see what many did not.”

2. Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life by Gerald Martin
(Bloomsbury)

“Remarkable … Martin’s assessments of Vargas Llosa’s books vary widely, but his praise of the ‘truly great’ writer is consistent. He is loyal to the man too, but that loyalty is more critical, and it is hard sometimes to see that the life and the books have much in common. Perhaps they don’t. And perhaps this biography is all the better for that reason … Martin understands perfectly that to explain is often to explain away.”
–Michael Wood (The New York Times Book Review)

3. The Sensualist: Adventures in Pure Pleasure by Gary Shteyngart
(Random House)

“As befits a sensualist, his style is deeply pleasurable, great lolloping sentences meeting the punchline of a short one, the jokes generous and surprising. The tone is confiding, charming, often unreservedly silly.”

4. The Imperfect City: Design, Serendipity, and the Real Life of Cities by Paul Goldberger
(Knopf)

3 Rave • 2 Positive
Read an excerpt from The Imperfect City here

“Fascinating, in-depth … Goldberger offers architecture aficionados a robust consideration of how these cities evolved, but also a new angle for history buffs and a pleasure for both world and armchair travelers.”

5. Notes on Postcards: A Memoir by Jennifer Croft
(Catapult)

2 Rave • 2 Positive
Read an excerpt from Notes on Postcards here

“..an earnest, elegant meditation on place and purpose … The book presents life, appealingly, as a concatenation of everywhere one has been, all that has happened–and positions the translator as linguistic and cultural go-between. In paring her story back to the basics, Croft has produced something that, much like a postcard, is simultaneously ‘telltale and intimate…ephemeral and lasting.’”
